name: Hong Kong
why: OpenRice is Hong Kong's restaurant review standard.

spots.name: Central Plaza
spots.desc: Can be seen from most of Wan Chai. Central Plaza was the tallest building in Asia from 1992 to 1996, and the tallest in Hong Kong until 2003. It is possible to tell the time by the changing lights on the top of this building. During business hours, you can take the lift from the ground floor to the sky lobby on the 46th floor to get a spectacular free view of the harbour and the island. Another…

spots.name: Hong Kong Disneyland
spots.desc: Asia's second Disneyland was opened in September 2005 and features some of the Disney favourites. The park is accessible via the MTR. Change at the Sunny Bay station on the Tung Chung MTR line for the Disneyland Resort Line. It has nine themed areas: Main Street USA, Adventureland, Fantasyland, Tomorrowland, Toy Story Land, Grizzly Gulch, Mystic Point, World of Frozen and Stark Expo. Tickets are…

spots.name: Tian Tan Buddha
spots.desc: At over 250 tonnes and 34 m in height, this was the largest seated outdoor bronze Buddha statue in the world, until the statue of Dordenna Buddha near Thimphu in Bhutan was finished in 2015. The site also offers unobstructed views over the island. Access to the Buddha is free, although entering the museum inside during busy times requires a meal ticket for the vegetarian restaurant; a snack costs…

spots.name: Tai Mo Shan
spots.desc: The highest point in Hong Kong, at about 956 m above sea level or 957 m above the Hong Kong Principal Datum. You hike almost to the summit, but not all the way as the summit houses a weather station and military outpost.

spots.name: Mong Kok
spots.desc: With a population density of 130,000/km2, Mong Kok is described as the busiest district in the world. It is characterised by a mixture of old and new multi-story buildings, with shops and restaurants at street level, and commercial or residential units above. (The shops on upper floors, which tourists may miss, often sell things cheaper.) Many of Mong Kok's streets have acquired nicknames…

spots.name: Kowloon Mosque and Islamic Centre
spots.local: 九龍清真寺暨伊斯蘭中心
spots.desc: The largest mosque in Hong Kong.
spots.addr: No. 105, Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Clock Tower
spots.local: 尖沙咀鐘樓, Former Kowloon-Canton Railway Clock Tower
spots.desc: Built out of red bricks and granite, the Clock Tower peaks at 44 metres, and is topped by a 7-metre lightning rod. The top of the tower can be reached by a wooden staircase located within.

spots.name: Avenue of Stars
spots.desc: A promenade to honour celebrities of the Hong Kong film industry, modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

spots.name: Kowloon Park
spots.desc: the location of a former British barrack. There, you will find not only pleasant gardens, but aviaries, museums, and sporting facilities, including Hong Kong's best swimming pool complex, which offers both indoor and outdoor pools. A wide range of swimming, diving and children's play-pools will appeal to kids of all ages, and their frazzled parents who are seeking a safe place for youngsters to…

spots.name: Hong Kong Park
spots.desc: A great place to relax in Central. Head for L16 cafe and bar which is one of the few places where you can eat and drink outdoors away from the traffic.

spots.name: Jamia Mosque
spots.desc: Constructed in 1890, it is the oldest mosque in Hong Kong.

spots.name: Hong Kong Space Museum
spots.desc: Small museum, with a basic history of space flight in static exhibits, including a single exhibit on Chinese space flight. It also has interactive exhibits, allowing you to fly a hang glider, work a space motion system, and simulate walking on the moon. It has a planetarium attached that shows movies projected onto the roof. Plan ahead if you want to see an English session, as most are Cantonese.…
spots.hours: Mon Wed-Sat noon-8:45PM, Sun 10AM-8:45PM, Tue closed
spots.price: $10 on most days. Free on Wednesdays

spots.name: Hong Kong Heritage Museum
spots.desc: For those with a serious interest in Chinese culture, this might appeal to you as one of Hong Kong's best museums. Modern, informative and attractively presented, this museum houses several permanent exhibitions of life in the New Territories, Cantonese opera, and Chinese art, as well as temporary exhibitions of a high calibre.
spots.hours: Mon Wed-Fri 10AM-6PM, Sat Sun 10AM-7PM (closed Tue plus first ane second day of Chinese New Year)

spots.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
spots.desc: The permanent exhibition, the Hong Kong Story, covers the history of Hong Kong from millions of years ago until the reunification with China in 1997. Exhibits are about the nature, culture and history of Hong Kong. Also special exhibitions changing every few months. Forget the idea that all of Hong Kong museums are frumpy and boring. The Hong Kong Story is a real must go and do, ideal for those…
spots.addr: 100 Chatham Rd South, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Chungking Mansions
spots.desc: Houses many budget Indian, Nepali and African restaurants. Touts at the front entrance will lead you to the restaurants via the small rickety lifts. Be warned that the competition between the touts can become very open, sometimes aggressive, so you should be prepared to make your choice as quickly as possible to avoid being dragged away to a restaurant that you did not really plan on going to.…

spots.name: Ngong Ping 360
spots.desc: A spectacular 5.7-km cable car journey that takes in an impressive cultural themed village and the Tian Tan Buddha. At the themed village there are a couple of attractions. The Walking with Buddha attraction gives an interesting introduction to Buddha, and has different stages, with headphones giving the narration in a variety of languages. The Monkey's Tail is simply a silent animated movie…

spots.name: Lantau Peak
spots.desc: At 934 m, the second highest point in Hong Kong and the highest point on Lantau Island. You can also stay overnight at the Ngong Ping hostel, and wake up very early to reach the summit in time for the spectacular sunrise. Although not particularly high by international standards, this is a fairly hard climb and you should make full preparations, especially during summer.

spots.name: Hong Kong Wetland Park
spots.desc: Is a relaxing park set amidst an ecological mitigation area. One can stroll along a network of board walks built over the marshy area and watch birds from a tower. The park also features a large visitors centre/museum. The museum has many interactive exhibits ideal for children, as well as some live animal habitats. To visit, take MTR West Rail to Tin Shui Wai Station, then the #705 light rail to…

spots.name: Victoria Park
spots.desc: Take some time to walk through it or to watch people play football on three fields. There is also a jogging track through the park. Victoria Park can also be reached by MTR Exit B at Tin Hau station. During the summer months you can use the public open-air pool in Victoria Park. The pool costs $19 for adults ($9 kids) and payment can be made by coins or Octopus card.

spots.name: Hong Kong Central Library
spots.desc: Opened in 2001, Hong Kong's main public library looks over the playgrounds of Victoria Park. It is an impressive 12-storey structure that holds a vast collection of Chinese and English resources. Visitors will find exhibitions, wifi access, newspapers and magazines. There is a souvenir shop and a branch of Delifrance where you can relax.

spots.name: The Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre
spots.desc: One of Hong Kong's most outstanding buildings. If you are refused admittance, you can take a walk along the promenade at the front of the building to find the place where the British returned Hong Kong to mainland China. Paved in concrete, the modest plaza where the Handover took place in 1997 is home to two monuments; one takes the form of a giant golden bauhinia and the other looks like a…

spots.name: Ohel Leah Synagogue
spots.desc: Orthodox synagogue built by Baghdadi Jews in 1902. Most of Hong Kong's Jewish community lives in the surrounding neighbourhood.

spots.name: Central-Mid-Levels Escalator
spots.desc: At 800 m long, this is the longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. The escalator runs downhill from 6AM to 10AM and uphill from 10:30AM to midnight every day. Part of it near the bottom goes along Cochrane Street, and it's hard to miss. It goes from busy areas at the bottom to upscale residential neighborhoods at the top. For tourists it's not all that useful for transportation…

spots.name: A Symphony of Lights
spots.desc: The narration is in English M-W-F, Mandarin Tu-Th-Sa and Cantonese Su. You can also download the app for your preferred narration.

spots.name: Nathan Road
spots.desc: Tsim Sha Tsui's main artery. Packed with stores, particularly cheap electronics shops. Be careful when shopping here; these slippery guys know every trick in the book and some stores are notorious for overcharging tourists. Locals seldom go to Tsim Sha Tsui for electronic products. It is more advisable to go to Mong Kok or Sham Shui Po instead.

spots.name: Po Lin Monastery
spots.desc: The monastery was founded in 1906 by three monks from Jiangsu province. The main temple building houses three bronze statues representing the Buddha of the past, present and future.

spots.name: Hong Kong Railway Museum
spots.desc: An open-air museum converted from the old Tai Po Railway Station. It has seven railway coaches and two locomotives.
spots.hours: Open from 10AM-6PM on Mon and Wed-Sunday. Closing is 1 hour earlier (5PM) on Christmas Eve and Lunar New Year's Eve.…
spots.addr: 13 Shung Tak Street, Tai Po Market, Tai Po

spots.name: 10,000 Buddhas Monastery
spots.desc: This rather garish but enjoyable modern temple dating from the 1950s in fact contains no less than 12,800 Buddhas lining the walls of the main hall. There's also a nine-story pagoda and some smaller temples above the main complex. Half the fun is getting there, the 500-metre path that climbs up the hill is lined with life-sized golden plastic statues of Buddhas in poses ranging from serene to…

spots.name: Ocean Park
spots.desc: A huge Disney-like (in both the good and bad sense) oceanarium. Marine biodiversity in the Atoll Reef and Shark Tank, and thrill rides will satisfy children and adults alike. It is popular with locals as well as tourists from mainland China. It has beautiful views from the cable car over the ocean and hills. The cablecar is an icon and an essential link between the two parts of the park. The view…

spots.name: Langham Place
spots.desc: Langham Place is an entertainment complex comprising of a 15-storey shopping mall, a 59-level Grade A office tower and the 5-star Langham Place Hotel. Over 300 shops where you will find everything from fashion labels to casual wear, from accessories to electronics. On special occasions, large crowds will gather under the 'Digital Sky' to celebrate festive events such as the New Year's Eve…

spots.name: Sham Shui Po
spots.desc: Has the largest number of computer and electronics shops.

spots.name: City Hall
spots.desc: Concert hall, theatre, and exhibition space. This cultural hub is famous for its dim sum restaurant.

spots.name: Inspiration Lake Recreation Centre
spots.desc: Inspiration Lake is the largest artificial lake in Hong Kong, and has a 1500-m jogging trail. It also has an arboretum, and rents paddle boats and surrey bikes. It is in Penny's Bay, a 15-minute walk from Disneyland Resort MTR station, or take the R8 bus.

spots.name: Noon Day Gun
spots.desc: The historic gun is fired every day at noon and once a year at midnight on New Year's Eve. To access the Noon Day Gun, enter the underground tunnel between the World Trade Centre and the Excelsior Hotel and follow the signs. Finding this tunnel is difficult and you might need to ask staff for directions. The tradition of firing a gun into Victoria Harbour everyday at noon dates back to the 1860s.…

spots.name: The Museum of Coastal Defence
spots.local: 香港抗戰及海防博物館
spots.desc: Despite its dry title, this museum is worth a visit if you enjoy military history.
spots.addr: 175 Tung Hei Road, Shau Kei Wan

spots.name: Ammar Mosque and Osman Ramju Sadick Islamic Centre
spots.desc: The third mosque built in Hong Kong.
spots.addr: No. 40, Oi Kwan Road, Wan Chai

spots.name: Chai Wan Mosque
spots.desc: The fifth mosque built in Hong Kong.
spots.addr: Cape Collison Road, Tai Tam Gap, Chai Wan

spots.name: Cenotaph
spots.desc: Built in 1923 in honour of the fallen soldiers of World War I and later also attributed to the ones from World War II. It is a copy of the more famous one in London. There is a ceremony on on the second Sunday of November to commemorate the fallen soldiers.

spots.name: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens
spots.desc: A small, free zoo with reptiles, primates, a jaguar, and rare and endangered birds and plants.

spots.name: Hong Kong Coliseum
spots.desc: Multi-purpose indoor arena with 12,500 seats. A famous landmark shaped almost like an upside down pyramid. Used for sport events, concerts and other things.

spots.name: Golden Bauhinia Square
spots.desc: The site of the ceremony in 1997 in which the United Kingdom returned Hong Kong to China. A flag raising ceremony is held here ever morning at 8AM, when the Hong Kong Police will perform foot drills and raise both the Chinese national flag and the Hong Kong flag to the accompaniment of the Chinese national anthem. Visit at night time for a stunning view of the neon-lit skylines of Kowloon and…

spots.name: Government House
spots.desc: Originally the official residence of the British Governors of Hong Kong under colonial rule, since the handover back to China in 1997, it has been the official residence of the Chief Executive of Hong Kong. Only open to the public on specific open days that are usually published on the web-site in advance, usually once in the spring to coincide with the blooming of the flowers in the garden, and…

spots.name: Kowloon Walled City Park
spots.desc: The Kowloon Walled City began as an enclave that remained under Chinese sovereignty when the New Territories and the rest of Kowloon were ceded to the British. After the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912, its legal status became disputed, and there was no effective government within the walled city as a result. The massive influx of mainland Chinese refugees after the communist takeover led to…
spots.addr: Tung Tau Tsuen Road, Kowloon City

spots.name: Hong Kong Police Museum
spots.desc: There are five galleries: Orientation describing the history of the force, Triad Societies and Narcotics describing the history of Triad Societies and narcotic problems, Police Then & Now describing the transformation of Hong Kong Police Force over the years, Current Exhibition exhibiting changing themes, and Heroin Factory exhibiting a heroin production site.

spots.name: Hong Kong Cricket Club
spots.desc: Private club but one restaurant is open to the public. If you're a cricket player, you can apply to join as a sports member.

spots.name: Hong Kong Film Archive
spots.addr: 50 Lei King Road, Sai Wan Ho

spots.name: Statue Square
spots.desc: Public square built in the 19th century with a number of royal statues. Now the only statue is of banker Sir Thomas Jackson. It is a relaxing place with plantings and fountains. The square is surrounded by some impressive buildings, including the HSBC headquarters and the Legislative Council.

spots.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
spots.desc: A museum displaying artefacts from the Forbidden City in Beijing.
spots.hours: Mon Wed Thu 10AM-6PM, Fri Sat Sun 10AM-8PM
spots.price: Adults $50, concessions $25, entry is free on Wednesdays provided you book online
spots.addr: 8 Museum Drive, West Kowloon Cultural District (西九文化區博物館道8號)

spots.name: Nan Lian Garden
spots.desc: A Tang-dynasty-style garden, part of the Chi Lin Nunnery complex.

spots.name: Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground
spots.local: Mission Road Ground, 天光道遊樂場
spots.desc: With a capacity of 3500, this is the home stadium of the Hong Kong national cricket team, who play separately from China.
spots.addr: Tin Kwong Rd, Ma Tau Wai

spots.name: Fa Yuen Street
spots.desc: This street is famous for selling sport gear, with over fifty stores selling sport shoes.
spots.addr: Fa Yuen St, between Boundary St and Dundas St

spots.name: Maclehose Trail
spots.desc: Stage I is ~3 hours, stage II ~6 hours of walking for a total of 10 stages and 100km. Parts are sealed/concrete road, other parts dirt/rock. if you hike late, take a light as public lights are sparse. Altitude is between 0 and 300m (Sai Wan Shan). Camping sites are available.

spots.name: Law Uk Folk Museum
spots.desc: 18th-century Hakka village house.

spots.name: Kwan Kung Pavilion
spots.desc: A smaller temple perched atop a hill. The temple is dedicated to the general Kwan Kung, who is most commonly associated with fraternities.

spots.name: Tung Choi Street
spots.desc: Hong Kong's biggest outdoor shopping experience. Prices here may not be the cheapest, as the area is popular with tourists, but the variety, chaos and sheer number of sellers is mind-boggling and well worth the visit. It is also opened during daytime, unlike the nearby Temple Street Night Market. As with other markets lacking fixed prices, those perceived as being tourists will be quoted a higher…
spots.addr: Tung Choi St, between Sai Yeung Choi St and Fa Yuen St

spots.name: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
spots.desc: Different rock formations and geological features are found here.The park is an area of 150 km2 across parts of the eastern and northeastern New Territories.

spots.name: Kat Hing Wai
spots.desc: Of more historical than practical interest, this tiny walled village was one of the first settlements of the Tang clan, who arrived in Hong Kong in the 12th century and have dominated much of the area ever since. The village today, however, has lots of nondescript modern low-rise concrete housing blocks crammed behind a crumbling gray brick wall. $1 donation requested, and if you see the old…

spots.name: Lam Tsuen Wishing Tree
spots.desc: The Wishing Tree is an old tree. Traditionally, it is believed that it will bring good luck and fortune. Nowadays, it is a tourist spot for both Westerners and locals. Simply go to Tai Po Market Railway Station and take the green minibus route 25K, or bus 64K to get to the Wishing Tree. Alternatively, you are advised to take a green taxi from Tai Wo Railway Station if you have 4 or 5 people…

spots.name: New Town Plaza
spots.desc: This is a huge shopping complex in Sha Tin which sells mid-range goods of all types. Well worth a visit but it will be crowded on weekends. Accessible through the Shatin MTR station, change at Kowloon Tong or Hung Hom station if travelling from Kowloon and Admiralty station if travelling from Hong Kong island. It also connects with a few nearby but smaller shopping malls via the footbridge…
spots.addr: 17-18 Sha Tin Centre St, Sha Tin

spots.name: The Old Wan Chai Post Office
spots.desc: Now an Environmental Resource Centre, this building was used for over 70 years as a post office. This attractive building is the only declared monument in Wan Chai.

spots.name: Quarry Bay Park
spots.desc: A good place to walk that provides an alternative view of the eastern end of the harbour, instead of the familiar one of the west. It also serves as a connection between SOHO east (a reasonably attractive restaurant and pub area) and Cityplaza shopping centre.

spots.name: City Gallery
spots.desc: A celebration of planning proposals and infrastructure projects. Interactive features and devices give visitors the latest information on planning and infrastructure developments in Hong Kong.

spots.name: Cheung Po Tsai Cave
spots.desc: A deep cave system which is rumoured to be where the famous pirate Cheung Po Tsai (張保仔) once hid his loot, although nothing has ever been found.

spots.name: The Cheung Chau Bun Festival
spots.desc: It is a popular annual event held in early May, this is a festival where people climb up a tower which is covered with buns. The event was abolished because a tower collapsed and injured 24 people in 1978 under immense weight by people climbing onto it. However, thanks to the people who live in Cheung Chau, who campaigned for many years, the government allowed this component of the festival to…

spots.name: Hong Kong Heritage Discovery Centre
spots.desc: Housed in former British colonial barracks, which are architecturally interesting in their own right. The centre houses one permanent (Explore our Heritage) and a couple of temporary exhibitions about Hong Kong's and China's history. There are also lectures, workshops and similar events.
spots.addr: Kowloon Park, Haiphong Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Sai Yeung Choi Street South
spots.desc: A street full of shops selling consumer electronic products, cosmetics, and discount books.

spots.name: Yuen Po Street Bird Garden
spots.desc: Hundreds of songbirds in exquisitely crafted cages can be seen at this market.

spots.name: Castle Peak Monastery
spots.desc: Classed as a Grade I historic building that has been standing for more than 1000 years. These historic monuments have stood through the ages in a tranquil woodland area. The striking and picturesque surroundings create an enjoyable view, as well as a solemn ambiance. Upon entering the monastery, you will notice the words "香海名山" (Fragrant Sea and Prestigious Mountain) engraved on the portico. The…

spots.name: Miu Fat Buddhist Monastery
spots.desc: This is a temple built in 1960 and is one of the best monasteries for visitors to enjoy.

spots.name: Sam Tung Uk Museum
spots.desc: A Hakka walled-village that was built in 1786.

spots.name: Hong Kong Correctional Services Museum
spots.desc: The museum has been extensively renovated with 10 galleries including a mock gallows, two replicas of prison cells and more than 600 separate exhibits including historical documents, photographs and artifacts from the history of Hong Kong's prison system. An annex also displays examples of products made by prisoners at the nearby Stanley Prison.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 10:00 to 17:00 except on public holidays

spots.name: Hike the Dragon's Back
spots.desc: A 2-3 hour hiking trail with spectacular views of the south of Hong Kong Island. The ridge has little shade and you should take a lot of water and protection in summer. The path then drops into forests and creeks, before emerging at Big Wave Bay, where you can swim, eat, drink and return on the same number 9 bus.

spots.name: Yuk Hui Temple
spots.desc: Possibly the most famous temple on Cheung Chau due to its connection with the Cheung Chau Bun Festival, which is held every year.

spots.name: Elements
spots.desc: Opened in 2007, Elements is Hong Kong's latest mega-mall. Aimed at wealthy shoppers, it has five themed shopping zones: Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth. Owned by the MTR Corporation, the shops are located above Kowloon MTR station. Probably not worth going out of your way for, but it does have some of the most extravagant public toilets in Hong Kong.
spots.addr: 1 Austin Road West, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Goldfish Street
spots.desc: Dozens of shops selling tropical freshwater and marine fish, aquariums and accessories.

spots.name: Apliu Street
spots.desc: A collection of market stalls where you can find phones, small electronic devices and DIY tools. Even if you are not that interested in electronic bric-à-brac, the pedestrianised streets in the area have a buzz about them that make a visit interesting.
spots.addr: Apliu St, between Yen Chow St and Nam Cheong St

spots.name: Sin Tat Shopping Centre
spots.desc: If you're after a new phone, this mall is home to many sellers with a wide selection, from iPhones to Japanese imports.

spots.name: Temple Street
spots.desc: South of Mong Kok is a great place to eat Chinese street food. You have not been to Honkers unless you have eaten in this street. Temple Street, famously featured in Chinese cinema, is one of the few pedestrianised streets in Kowloon where you can sit, relax and watch the world pass by. Seafood is a popular choice, but most restaurants will provide you with an extensive English/Chinese menu that…

spots.name: Ping Shan Heritage Trail
spots.desc: This is a kilometre long trail enabling you to take in the most important buildings in this historical area, including the ancient pagoda of Tsui Sing Lau, the Tang Ancestral Hall and the Kun Ting Study Hall.

spots.name: Ching Chung Koon
spots.desc: A traditional Taoist temple. Many people go to here to worship the gods.

spots.name: Southorn Playground
spots.local: 修頓遊樂場, 修頓球場
spots.desc: Amidst the skyscrapers of Wan Chai, Southorn Playground offers a scarce area of public outdoor space for football, basketball and has seating for those who just want to relax and watch.

spots.name: Gloucester Road
spots.desc: Pronounced in the British way as Gloss-ter Road, this street is famous for car showrooms where the rich will spend and the rest will take photographs of themselves in front of their dream car.

spots.name: Hung Shing Ye Beach
spots.desc: This is a nice beach close to Yung Shue Wan. It is somewhat overshadowed by having a coal fired Power Plant in the background.

spots.name: Cheung Chau Mini Great Wall
spots.desc: Constructed in 1997 by the Home Affairs Department, it is a part of the Cheung Chau Family Trail. The name “Mini Great Wall” is given from the line of granite railings which looks similar to the Great Wall of China. The trail passes by a variety of specially-shaped rocks including the Loaf Rock, the Rock of Ringing Bell, the Eagle Rock, Fa Peng Rock, Human Head Rock, Rock of the Skull, Yuk Saai…

spots.name: Golden Computer Centre
spots.desc: The largest computer mall in Hong Kong, with both hardware and software vendors competing extremely vigorously. This is a Mecca for the nerdy-trainspotter-types who salivate over the latest gadget.

spots.name: Jockey Club Kau Sai Chau Public Golf Course
spots.desc: Hong Kong's only public golf course, comprising three 18-hole courses. Accessible by ferry from Sai Kung.

spots.name: Ma On Shan Plaza
spots.desc: A large shopping plaza in Ma On Shan with a variety of stores. The items are more affordable as the plaza is located in a less-affluent area. It has a series of footbridges that connect to other shopping complexes such as Sunshine City Plaza and MOSTown. Accessible through Ma On Shan MTR station, change at Tai Wai or Diamond Hill if travelling from Kowloon and Hong Kong Island.
spots.addr: Ma On Shan Plaza, 608 Sai Sha Rd, Ma On Shan, Hong Kong

spots.name: Lung Wah Hotel
spots.desc: It is famous for roasted pigeons.

spots.name: Stanley Ma Hang Park
spots.desc: Opened in January 2011. This 50,000-m² park is set into the cliffside near Murray House. It features boardwalks, a butterfly garden, a fitness deck, bird watching platforms, an educational trail and the cliffside Pak Tai Temple.

spots.name: Cheung Chau Rock Carving
spots.desc: A series of carvings made into rocks on the island that are, as yet, of unknown age, but are said to resemble pottery which dates from the Bronze Age.

spots.name: Hung Shing Temple
spots.desc: A smaller temple building that was constructed in 1813; the current structure has been renovated and repaired several times since then.

spots.name: Cheung Chau Sports Ground
spots.desc: The local sports stadium which contains a green as well as a running track. It is the only sports ground in the Islands District.

spots.name: Pak She Tin Hau Temple
spots.desc: The temple contains a copper bell which was cast in 1767.

spots.name: Lok Fu Centre
spots.desc: Located in a public housing estate, goods here are generally more affordable than in other places. There is also a large department store here.

spots.name: Café "1974"
spots.desc: A coffee shop operated by Po Leung Kuk that also functions as the ICAC's museum. The shop was named after the year of establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, and coffee is known to be one of the drinks available to detainees during interrogation. Good coffee at around $22.
spots.addr: G/F, ICAC Building, 303 Java Road, North Point

spots.name: Yung Kee
spots.desc: An outlet of the once Michelin one-starred restaurant Yung Kee in Central, the place is prized for its charcoal-roasted goose and Cantonese double-stewed soups. However, besides its goose, Yung Kee is also well known for preserving traditional and authentic Cantonese flavors. If you need to eat airside and have money to burn, Yung Kee should be your top priority.
spots.addr: Food Court near Gate 40-80, Departures Level (L6), Terminal 1

spots.name: Dialogue in the Dark
spots.desc: An exhibition in complete darkness. Experience five different Hong Kong themed environments using your non-visual senses on a 75-minute tour with the help of a visually impaired guide. Reservations are recommended, especially for a tour in English or Mandarin instead of Cantonese.
spots.price: Weekdays $160, $90 for students and seniors; weekends $180, $100 for students and seniors
spots.addr: Shop 215, 2/F, The Household Centre, Nob Hill, 8 King Lai Path, Mei Foo

spots.name: Temple Street Night Market
spots.desc: Encompasses a block of streets in Kowloon barricaded at the end of each day with stalls selling almost anything until midnight. You can buy the usual touristy stuff, but there are also bargains like Chinese silk pajamas, toys, electronics and cheap leather goods. Arrive at Yau Ma Tei MTR Station Exit C, then walk up Man Ming Lane to Temple Street after nightfall. Be prepared to bargain vigorously…

spots.name: The Bridge
spots.desc: Considered to have the best views among the airport's lounges, reopened in 2025 after extensive renovations, with an ambience similar to that of The Pier. Divided into two sections, the right side has a selection of Western dishes and a bar with alcoholic drinks, mocktails and barista coffee. The left side has Cathay Pacific's signature noodle bar, some dim sum and a selection of other Chinese…

spots.name: The Pier
spots.desc: Widely regarded to be the nicest of Cathay Pacific's lounges, and a contender for the best airport lounge in the world. The business class section features a bar with a selection of alcoholic beverages and mocktails, a Western food counter with wood-fired pizza a selection of premium European cured meats, Cathay Pacific's signature noodle bar and a tea room with barista coffee and a selection of…

spots.name: The Wing
spots.desc: Cathay Pacific's flagship lounge, with a newly-renovated first class section featuring a-la-carte dining and complimentary massage, with a special speakeasy-like area reserved explicitly for Cathay Pacific's own first class and diamond frequent flyer passengers. The business class section is temporarily closed for renovation.

spots.name: Plaza Premium Lounge
spots.desc: 2 pay-per-use lounges airside, one near Gate 1 and one near Gate 40, which are also available to people with membership in programmes such as Diners' Club and Priority Pass. All lounges feature a noodle bar where you can order hot dishes, including their signature fish ball noodles.
spots.price: 2 hours $580, 1 hour shower and breakfast package $280

spots.name: American Express Centurion lounge
spots.desc: American Express operates a Centurion lounge that is available to people with American Express Platinum or Centurion credit cards.

spots.name: Ho Hung Kee
spots.desc: A branch of the famous Ho Hung Kee restaurant in Causeway Bay, this eatery was awarded one Michelin star in 2010. The place is most prized for its noodles, especially for its beef chow foon and wonton noodles, but also offers an extraordinary selection of Cantonese food in general. If you arrive at Terminal 1, Ho Hung Kee is strongly recommended.

spots.name: Crystal Jade La Mian Xiao Long Bao
spots.desc: Crystal Jade is a chain Shanghai restaurant that has been, at one point, included in the Michelin Guide for Hong Kong and Macau, although without receiving a star. The place offers a variety of Shanghainese foods, but is most famous for its xiao long bao (juicy pork dumplings) and noodles. If you need a break from Cantonese food, you may give this place a try.

spots.name: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
spots.desc: Opened in 1989 and in a prominent position on the waterfront, it is a contender for being the most famous ugly building in Hong Kong. However, if you are a lover of the arts, don't judge this building by its bland exterior; inside the architects have created a superb space that really does justice to the sights and sounds of each performance.

spots.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
spots.desc: A fascinating, strange and elusive place. The entrance lies up one floor, mimicking the “temple” approach to the high altar of culture and art. Once you arrive on the first floor, you are bathed in light from the wall of glass that gives you a panoramic view of Hong Kong Island. The objects on show are Chinese ceramics, terracotta, rhinoceros horn and Chinese paintings. There is also a temporary…

spots.name: Hong Kong Science Museum
spots.desc: Large museum with many interactive exhibits including an energy machine and an airplane. A museum which decided to make an architectural statement about its purpose, yet somehow got it horribly wrong. This museum is primarily aimed at children. The maths puzzles and optical illusions on the top floor are challenging. There is a giant Rube Goldberg machine spanning the entire museum that is run…
spots.addr: 2 Science Museum Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui East

spots.name: Lei Cheng Uk Han Tomb Museum
spots.desc: Tomb from the Eastern Han dynasty (AD 25 - 220) discovered in 1955. Exhibition hall displaying pottery and artifacts from the excavation of the tomb.

spots.name: M+
spots.desc: Museum of contemporary visual culture (architecture, design, animation, and visual art) with a local and global focus.

spots.name: Shek Kip Mei Estate
spots.desc: Built in the 1950s, this is one of the few remaining places where you can grasp the living conditions of Hong Kong during the 50s and 60s. Despite the march of progress promulgated by the Urban Renewal Authority, there are still a few blocks of flats remaining from the 1950s, which are still occupied. Walk from Shek Kip Mei MTR Station.

spots.name: Shanghai Street
spots.desc: runs north-south parallel to Nathan Road and offers an easy to navigate urban transect. Start at the north-side of Kowloon Park and wander up to Langham Place, a modern shopping and hotel complex which is next to Mong Kok MTR station. Along the way you will experience Kowloon in its raw authenticity. This is not your regular tourist trail, but crumbling tenements and small-scale industrial and…

spots.name: Marine Police Headquarters
spots.desc: Dating back to 1884, it is an attractive colonial building that has been renovated to become a major tourism attraction with shops and restaurants.

spots.name: Sik Sik Yuen Wong Tai Sin Temple
spots.desc: Next to Wong Tai Sin MTR Station, this is the most popular Taoist temple in Hong Kong. This is where many people ask for divine guidance by a practice known as kau cim (求籤), a practice that has all but disappeared in mainland China. Entrance is free, though voluntary donations are welcome.

spots.name: Kowloon Park Swimming Pool Complex
spots.desc: Offers a wide range of services, including an indoors Olympic-sized pool, a slightly smaller training pool, a diving pool, and a leisure pool for younger swimmers. During the summer months, the indoor pools are air-conditioned, whilst in winter the water is heated. During the summer season, there are four outdoor leisure pools that are popular with teenagers, but all age-groups make good use of…

spots.name: Festival Walk
spots.desc: Festival Walk is another excellent shopping mall in the suburb of Kowloon Tong. A very pleasant place to shop, similar to Pacific Place but catering more to locals.

spots.name: Harbour City
spots.desc: The largest shopping mall in Hong Kong. It is next to the Star Ferry pier. There are shops of almost any description there. The goods are mostly mid price range to high price brand name goods. The views of the bay are especially good from here at night.

spots.name: Flower Market Road
spots.desc: The street and the nearby side streets are packed with florists and street vendors selling flowers and plants. Worth a visit even if shrubs aren't high on your shopping list.

spots.name: Cheung Sha Wan Road
spots.desc: Famous for garments. There are many shops selling clothes along Cheung Sha Wan Road. It is within walking distance from Sham Shui Po MTR Station. A number of bus routes also pass along Cheung Sha Wan Road.

spots.name: CitySuper
spots.desc: A local upscale supermarket chain with pan Asian, Western style food and has its own food court in Harbour City on Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui.
spots.addr: 3/F, Gateway Arcade, Harbour City, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Choi Lung Restaurant
spots.desc: A typical local Chinese restaurant offering dim sum and a Cantonese style dinner. Dim Sum starts from $4.80. It is a nightclub after seven with contemporary music.

spots.name: Dragon Centre Food Court
spots.desc: This food court provides a variety of Chinese, Southeast Asian and Western cuisines at attractive prices. Dishes range from $10 up.
spots.addr: 8/F, Dragon Centre, 37K Yen Chow Street, Sham Shui Po

spots.name: Fa Yuen Street Complex
spots.desc: A complex consisting of a wet market, cooked food centre, sports centre and a public library. It is a place where you can find cheap and genuine Hong Kong style food in Kowloon. There was only one small food stall open on a Sunday afternoon. Maybe better during the week?

spots.name: Mr. Wong's
spots.desc: This one is popular with exchange students in Hong Kong, offering all the food you can eat and all the beer you can drink.

spots.name: Swagat
spots.desc: On the first floor of Chungking Mansions, this is arguably one of the best Indian restaurants in Hong Kong.

spots.name: Tim Ho Wan
spots.desc: It is said to be the cheapest Michelin starred restaurant in the world, serving a variety of dim sum dishes starting at $10. Be prepared to wait one, two or even three hours if you come on a busy day (you get a numbered menu/ticket and can come back later).

spots.name: Jade Palace
spots.desc: A tasty and tourist-friendly dim sum spot. Order by selecting from a card (also in English), not from a cart. Try the shrimp and chive dumplings and the tripe in ginger soup. Dim sum served 11AM-3PM daily, dishes $16-40 each.
spots.addr: 4/F, Star House, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Red Ant
spots.desc: A modern bistro-like restaurant with a wide selection of light meals and snacks. No alcohol is served but there is a long list of fresh juices and teas.
spots.addr: G/F, 27 Ashley Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Yat Tung Heen
spots.desc: Cantonese dishes and dim sum, from traditional favourites to original creations.
spots.addr: Eaton Hotel, 380 Nathan Road, Kwun Chung

spots.name: Green
spots.desc: Contemporary cafe and restaurant located within the modern Hotel Icon. Lunch offers set menus with lobster, pasta and more. Nice desserts and wine list. The interior is beautiful, with one of the world's largest indoor vertical gardens.

spots.name: La Taverna Restaurant
spots.desc: Hong Kong's oldest Italian restaurant sits hidden in plain view at the end of busy Ashley Road. Stepping through the door is like stepping back in time to a Hong Kong of the past or at least an Italian version of it circa 1960s. Delicious pastas and meat dishes and risottos to die for. Well worth a visit as much as for a sense of Hong Kong history as the tasty Italian food. A true oasis of…

spots.name: Oi Man Sang
spots.desc: This outdoor kitchen may be the last outdoor food stall still cooking over the extreme heat of kerosene, wok hei-style. Expect to stand in line for a bit.
spots.addr: Sham Shui Po Building, 1A-1C Shek Kip Mei St

spots.name: Fook Lam Moon
spots.desc: The yum cha/dim sum is excellent. The service and decor is also impressive. Expect to pay around $55 per serve for the mid range dishes. The English menu is only a small subset of the Chinese menu so take along someone who can translate to increase your choice of dishes. Another

spots.name: Gaddi's
spots.desc: Arguably Hong Kong's leading restaurant that has delighted aficionados of French food and wine for over 80 years. This is the place where you can test your own command of the French language against French-speaking Chinese waiters. You will be disappointed if you are expecting great harbour views.
spots.addr: Peninsula Hotel, Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

spots.name: Morton's The Steakhouse
spots.desc: The Hong Kong location for this famous chain of American steakhouses, Morton's has one best in the city multiple times. With views overlooking the harbour, great service and classic cocktails - combined with thick steaks - makes Morton's a classy and classic experience.

spots.name: Nobu
spots.desc: The HK location for this exclusive Japanese restaurant. Nobu has delicate bento box lunches and decadent dinners and desserts. Remarkable service and drinks, and a view overlooking the Harbour that is worth the price. Dress nice and make a reservation if going for dinner.

spots.name: Aqua
spots.desc: Nearby at the top of the 1 Peking Road office building is an alternative and less touristy spot with equally impressive views. As well as a bar, they have a Japanese and Italian restaurant for those without a budget.

spots.name: Biergarten
spots.desc: This friendly German bar is one of the few places in Kowloon where you can find a good range of quality beers. Excellent German food is served — not just sausages and sauerkraut. Use Exit N2 at East Tsim Sha Tsui MTR station.

spots.name: Felix
spots.desc: Atop the Peninsula Hotel on Salisbury Rd, is known for its Philippe Starck interior and the views of the harbour skyline, whilst the men's bathroom has an impressive view up Nathan Road. According to legend, the world's first screwdriver was mixed up here, sampling this simple mix of orange juice and vodka will set you back around $100 a pop.

spots.name: Hutong
spots.desc: Hutong is a great place to get a good view of Hong Kong from the top floor of a business building. It's a Michelin starred restaurant with amazing food — try the signature crispy lamb breast with garlic and ginger.

spots.name: Knutsford Terrace
spots.desc: Near the Miramar hotel is perhaps best described as the 'Lang Kwai Fong' of Kowloon, and has a large number of bars and restaurants of variable quality that cater for mid-range budgets. A little smaller and less phrenetic than Lan Kwai Fong, but well worth the effort to poke your nose along this narrow street on a Saturday evening.

spots.name: Ashley Road
spots.desc: Between Nathan Road and the Ocean Terminal shopping mall, features many Western restaurants and bars.

spots.name: Mody Road/Centennial Garden
spots.desc: Close to many good hotels, this area of Tsim Sha Tsui offers a more relaxed environment for a drink. Here you will find bars and restaurants spilling out onto the pavement. Leave East Tsim Sha Tsui station at Exit P1, and head past the Kowloon Shangri-La hotel.

spots.name: Tung Choi Street
spots.desc: Between Prince Edward Road and Boundary Street, is one of Kowloon's up-and-coming bar strips. Few tourists or expats venture here, but there are nearly two dozen bars. Some specialize in karaoke while others have open fronts and extensive drink menus. Prince Edward MTR, exit A.

spots.name: The Deck
spots.desc: The smallest of Cathay's lounges.

spots.name: United Club
spots.price: US $59 if not United Club member

spots.name: Aberdeen Seafood Restaurant
spots.price: Eat outside on the pavement and watch the world pass you buy in this busy street for pedestrians. Serves goose and…

spots.name: Man Mo Temple
spots.desc: A temple built in the 1890s, it is regarded by many as a must-see tourist destination in Hong Kong.

spots.name: Tai O
spots.desc: A traditional fishing village with houses built on stilts over the sea. Tai O also called "Eastern Venice".

spots.name: Discovery Bay
spots.desc: As a residential district, Discovery Bay is not really a tourist destination. However, it boasts a 400-m beach, a golf and marina club for members and guests, meaning that the area attracts day trippers. It also holds festivals, including most notably, dragon boat races at the beach in May/June and a multicultural festival in November.

spots.name: Mui Wo
spots.local: traditional Chinese: 梅窩, Pinyin: Méiwō, lit. "plum nest"
spots.desc: a rural town on the eastern coast of Lantau Island. The main beach in Mui Wo is known as Silver Mine Bay (銀礦灣). There are fast and slow ferry services from Central to Mui Wo. Central - Mui Wo Ferry The fast ferry costs $25 and takes 30 minutes. The slow ferry costs $15, takes 50 minutes and you can go outside. The 3M bus takes you from Tung Chung to Mui Wo. There are a number of temples and old…

spots.name: The Stoep
spots.desc: Beachside restaurant with a good western menu and also specializes in serving South African dishes. Although the food is not the main attraction, the location of this restaurant makes it one of the best places to eat and drink in Hong Kong. Booking a table is advisable at weekends and Public Holidays.

spots.name: High Tide Restaurant
spots.desc: Authentic Thai restaurant. Located right on the beach front, you might think you're in Thailand. An ideal place to get refreshments after a lazy day on one of Hong Kong's best beaches.

spots.name: China Beach Club
spots.desc: Silvermine Bay (Mui Wo). Head for the beach in the bay and then carry on walking. Serves great food and drinks to the colonial crowd and locals alike. This is a doggie paradise in Hong Kong.

spots.name: The China Bear
spots.desc: Mui Wo. Walk off the ferry and turn left and you will see a cafe/bar next to the sea. If you are looking for a "full English" breakfast, or some western beer, then you have found the right place.

spots.name: Food Republic
spots.desc: A large food court that is incredibly busy at lunch and dinner times on weekends with a lot of mainlanders hungry after a hard day of shopping.

spots.name: Olea
spots.desc: With floor-to-ceiling glass windows of 7 m looking out to a man-made water and bamboo feature. Olea is a casual fine dining restaurant in the hotel and features an open Mediterranean kitchen, with a pizza oven and an array of various classic tapas and mezze dishes.

spots.name: Essence
spots.desc: Located on the lobby level, Essence was designed by a world famous interior designer Yasumichi Morita.It is the main dining venue in the hotel and features international cuisine through buffet and à la carte offerings.

spots.name: 360 Forest Grill & Restaurant Bar
spots.desc: Overlooking the cable car, 360 Forest Grill & Restaurant Bar offers alfresco dining in a peaceful, garden setting; only moments away from the hustle of Tung Chung. A wide range of a-la-cart grilled meats and fresh sea foods, three course buffet sets, and standard Asian and European dishes.

spots.name: Starz
spots.desc: There are few bar options in Tung Chung, and this is probably the best you are going to find.

spots.name: Red House
spots.desc: This is a memorial building to Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The house and the farm was where Dr. Sun Yat-sen planned to overthrow the Qing dynasty. It is named after its appearance, red bricks with plastering in red. The two-storey house is a combination of Chinese and Western architecture. Adjacent to the house is a garden commemorating Dr. Sun Yat Sen and is one of a few places in Hong Kong where the Flag…
spots.addr: Near Lung Mun Road, Tuen Mun. In the park. Near TM Public Riding School.

spots.name: The Art Museum, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
spots.desc: M-W F Sa from 10AM-5PM, Sunday and public holidays from 1:00-5PM, closed Th (except public holidays), New Year, Lunar New Year, Easter, and Christmas holidays. Admission is free.
spots.addr: Art Museum, Institute of Chinese Studies, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Sha Tin

spots.name: Tao Heung Museum of Food Culture
spots.desc: Museum displays cooking utensils, cutlery, spices from different time periods around the world and the food culture of Hong Kong. Advance online reservation is required. Each session lasts 75 minutes. Guide will narrate in Cantonese for 45 minutes followed by 30 minutes of free tour.
spots.hours: Tours Sat Sun holidays from 9:30AM to 5:15PM
spots.addr: 13 Au Pui Wan St, Fo Tan

spots.name: Sha Tau Kok Anti-Japanese War Memorial Hall
spots.desc: Opened in September 2022, this is the first comprehensive museum about the Second World War in Hong Kong. The museum is at the former home of the Luo Family, which was the first base of operations for Communist-led guerrilla fighters from the Mainland who came across the border to help resist the Japanese. At the present time, the museum is only accepting group visits and bookings are essential.…
spots.addr: 39 Sha Tau Kok Road (Shek Chung Au), Sha Tau Kok

spots.name: Sha Tin Racecourse
spots.desc: Participate in the most popular sport in Hong Kong at games held most Saturday afternoons from September to June. Regular stand seats $10, but a special package available to overseas tourists-only allows box access for $130-190.

spots.name: Tai Po Waterfront Park
spots.desc: The Tai Po Waterfront Park is the largest park in Tai Po District. The Park provides a wide range of facilities including a 1.2 long promenade, rest-gardens, sitting-out areas, a jogging trail with fitness stations, a cycling track and a 600-seat amphitheatre. There is also a 32.4-metre-high Lookout Tower in the Park. After visiting the tower, visitors may move on to the Insect House nearby. Take…

spots.name: Tai Mei Tuk
spots.desc: Tai Mei Tuk is famous for the natural view of Pat Sin Leng and Plover Cove Reservoir, the largest reservoir in Hong Kong. You can also make use of the free barbecue site in Tai Mei Tuk and the adjoining country park. Get off from Tai Po Market Railway Station and take bus 75K or green minibus 20C.

spots.name: Kam Shan Country Park
spots.desc: Kam Shan Country Park, also known as Monkey Hill, is famous for its wild monkeys. It is at the north of Kowloon and so can be easily accessed by taking the KMB route 72 or 81 from Kowloon or New Territories. A free barbecue site is available in the country park.

spots.name: Tai Po Megamall
spots.desc: A group of shopping malls in the district. It is less crowded than New Town Plaza. Easily accessible by MTR and KMB buses. Take bus K12 from Tai Po Market Railway Station. It can also be reached by the buses which terminates at Tai Po Central.
spots.addr: No.8 & 10 On Pong Road, Tai Po

spots.name: Tai Wo Shopping Mall
spots.desc: It is next to Tai Wo Station is a typical shopping centre in a public housing estate. Do not expect a variety choice of shops are available, but goods are at reasonable price because the target customers are local people.

spots.name: Hang Heung (恒香)
spots.desc: It is arguably Hong Kong's most famous Chinese bakery and famous among ethnic Chinese worldwide for its wife cakes (老婆餅). Other products include egg rolls (蛋卷) and almond biscuits (杏仁餅).

spots.name: Uptown Plaza
spots.desc: Next to Tai Po Market Railway Station is a regional shopping centre in Tai Po.

spots.name: Wo Sang
spots.desc: Next to Kei Lun Light rail station in Tuen Mun. It is famous for its traditional Hong Kong dishes. You can sit next to the kitchen and watch how they cook the fried dishes. The roast goose here is also famous.

spots.name: Learn Hop
spots.desc: Next to the Siu Hong MTR station. Located inside the Siu Hong Commercial Complex. It is famous for its choice of Guangdong, wonton and dumpling noodles. Also serves Zha jiang mian.

spots.name: Tai Po Hui Market
spots.desc: A modern complex of small stalls. The must-try items are fried pork chop noodles and fish ball noodles. Also, for as little as $10 a dish, you can choose from a variety of culinary styles, including local favourites and dishes from Shanghai, Japan and south Asia. Tai Po Hui Market cooked food centre is located near Tai Po Market MTR Station.

spots.name: Chan Kun Kee
spots.desc: Wo Che Estate, Sha Tin. A typical Dai Pai Dong in Hong Kong providing a variety of Cantonese dishes. Get off at Sha Tin Railway Station and take a taxi to Wo Che Estate.

spots.name: Cheung Wah Estate
spots.desc: Cooked Food Centre near Fanling MTR Station. It is a cooked food centre located in a public housing estate. Dishes start at $10 up.

spots.name: Pai Tau Restaurant
spots.desc: Pai Tau Rd, Sha Tin. This little eatery in a stretch of old shophouses near MTR Sha Tin offers basic Cantonese fare with lunch sets for around $25. No English menu, but the staff are happy to assist.

spots.name: Fu Ah Seafood Restaurant
spots.desc: The second-to-last in Sai Kung's seafood restaurant alley, this unassuming joint does good set meals for $150/person, with reasonably priced beer and no surprises in the bill.
spots.addr: G/F 27, Hoi Pong St, Sai Kung

spots.name: Dragon Inn Seafood Restaurant
spots.desc: is a famous seafood restaurant in Tuen Mun. The price is more valuable than Sai Kung and you can go to the Sam Shing market to choose your seafood which would provide more variation. It is ranked one of the best seafood restaurant in Hong Kong.
spots.addr: 19.5 Miles, Castle Peak Road, Tuen Mun

spots.name: Shanghai Po Po
spots.desc: One of the best chain restaurant to eat the Shanghainese food. It serves big dishes at a value price. It's famous for its dan dan noodles and hot and sour soup.
spots.addr: Shop 3207, Phase 1, Tuen Mun Town Plaza, 3 Tuen Lung Street, Tuen Mun

spots.name: Ho To Tai dumpling wonton noodle
spots.addr: G/F, no.67, On Ning Road, Yuen Long

spots.name: Deli France
spots.desc: Near the MTR.

spots.name: Pizza Hut
spots.desc: Near the MTR.

spots.name: Hemingway’s by the Bay
spots.desc: Beachside dining with 80 indoor seats, 86 outside.

spots.name: China Bear
spots.addr: G/F, Mui Wo Ctr, Mui Wo

spots.name: Mcsorley's Ale House
spots.addr: Shop G11A, G/F, D Deck, Discovery Bay

spots.name: Jockey Club Museum of Climate Change
spots.hours: Mon Tue Thu-Sat 09:30-17:00. Closed on Wednesdays, Sundays, public holidays and university holidays (including…
spots.addr: Yasumoto International Academic Park, 8th Floor, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin

spots.name: Tsz Shan Monastery Buddhist Art Museum
spots.local: 慈山寺佛教藝術博物館
spots.hours: 10:00-13:00 (last admission at 12:30), 14:00-17:00 (last admission at 16:30), closed on Mondays (except Mondays that…
spots.addr: No. 88, Universal Gate Road, Tai Po

spots.name: Horse racing
spots.desc: Horse racing has been taking place at Happy Valley racetrack since 1846. Happy Valley is particularly impressive during the evening meets with the surrounding skyscrapers lit up. Unless you know the right sort of people your best chance of getting into the races is by the public entrance. Entrance will cost you just a few dollars and you will have the advantage of being at ground level next to…

spots.name: Hong Kong Racing Museum
spots.desc: Artificats and some of the largest exhibits in the world next to the track of the Happy Valley Racecourse.
spots.addr: 2/F, Happy Valley Stand, Happy Valley Racecourse, Wong Nai Chung Rd, Happy Valley

spots.name: Sogo
spots.desc: A Japanese department store. As well as the standard fare of international label goods (clothes, electronics, home furnishings, etc), there is an excellent supermarket in the basement, which sells a variety of Asian foods.

spots.name: Times Square
spots.desc: A shopping centre in Causeway Bay with an excellent concentration of mid-price range shops and restaurants. CitySuper in the basement is one of Hong Kong's upmarket supermarkets, with a food court serving a variety of reasonably priced meals.

spots.name: Chinese Goods Centre Ltd
spots.desc: Forget the westernised shopping malls and head for this Chinese-style department store in North Point. Here you will find almost anything you might expect in a large department store except prices are extremely competitive. If you are looking to buy gifts with an oriental flavour this is worth a try.

spots.name: Chun Yeung Street
spots.desc: A local market near the North Point Tram terminus. You can find traditional Chinese food, especially Hokkien style food there. There is a variety of household items, clothes and fresh food there. It is a bazaar typical of many on Hong Kong Island.

spots.name: G.O.D
spots.desc: G.O.D. is a play on the Cantonese slang for "to live better". Here you will find a range of designer gifts and household items.
spots.addr: Sharp Street, East Entrance, Causeway Bay

spots.name: Fashion Walk
spots.desc: An indoor street with shops and a range of western and Asian restaurants.

spots.name: RC Outfitters
spots.desc: A good range of hiking and camping accessories, plus outdoor clothing at reasonable prices.
spots.addr: 2/F, Kin Tak Fung Commercial Bldg, 467-473 Hennessy Road, Causeway Bay

spots.name: Wan Chai Computer Centre
spots.desc: Although not the largest computer centre in Hong Kong, this one is above Wan Chai station with two floors of small shops selling computers, laptops, tablet, accessories, headphones, games, etc. It is also the easiest to get to on Hong Kong island. Some shops open from 10:30, although generally speaking it isn't worth to visit before midday.

spots.name: Chiu Yuen
spots.desc: Small and usually packed eatery serving up a wide range of simple fare, but the crowd-pullers are the beef brisket noodles (a scarcely believable $13) and the homemade giant fishball soup ($16). Other branches are in Aberdeen and Causeway Bay.

spots.name: Tsui Wah Restaurant
spots.desc: Clean and multilingual, this is a moderately priced cha chaan teng where even a non-Chinese speaker can easily explore. Aside from the typical cha chaan teng foods such as French toast, curry, baked rice, fried noodles, and Hong Kong style milk-tea, also try their famous fishball noodle in soup. Expect to share a table at peak hours.

spots.name: Tai Hing Roast Restaurant
spots.desc: A Cantonese BBQ eatery. Roast pork, roast piglet, BBQ pork, roast goose, soy sauce chicken are all hanging in the front display window, available to eat in or take out.
spots.addr: G/F, Shop J, Po Ming Bldg, 49-57 Lee Garden Rd, Causeway Bay.

spots.name: Loving Hut
spots.desc: Serving vegetarian and vegan fast food at affordable prices.
spots.addr: Shops B&C, G/F, The Hennessy, 256 Hennessy Rd

spots.name: Hokkaido Dairy Farm
spots.desc: Ham, eggs, toast and Japanese milk. Very good for a light breakfast or lunch.
spots.addr: Shop A-B, G/F, 211 Johnston Road, Wan Chai

spots.name: 3.6.9. Restaurant Shanghai
spots.desc: Great old style dive usually packed with locals especially at lunch. Shanghai style Chinese food, excellent and inexpensive Xaio Long Bao. About as authentic as you'll find in this part of the island.

spots.name: The Quarterdeck Club
spots.desc: Fenwick Pier, Wanchai. This is one of the few harbourside restaurants. Slightly spoiled by the land reclamation nearby

spots.name: The Flying Pan
spots.desc: On the corner of Lockhart Road and Luard Road. Look above Mes Amis and you will find the best place for breakfast and it's open all-day, everyday. This is the place where you can have a full-English washed down with a glass of lager at any time you prefer. It has an extensive menu catering for all preferences and a "frequent fryer" club if you want to keep going back. Staff are friendly and speak…

spots.name: Kung Tak Lam
spots.desc: A delightful vegetarian restaurant serving Shanghainese cuisine. Hotpot, dim sum and noodles dishes are made with MSG free ingredients.

spots.name: Red Pepper Restaurant
spots.desc: Causeway Bay (MTR: Causeway Bay). Sichuan cuisine; spicy dishes.

spots.name: Pho Saigon
spots.desc: Extremely good Vietnamese restaurant serving traditional dishes including Pho and Vietnamese coffee. Expect to pay around $120.

spots.name: Tai Ping Koon Restaurant
spots.desc: (太平館餐廳), 6 Pak Sha Road, Causeway Bay. Founded in Guangzhou in 1860, the three locations (two in Kowloon) have now become institutions of Canto-Western cuisine. Don't be put off by the touristy menu available in three languages, as the restaurant is very popular with locals. Some specialties are the Swiss sauce chicken wings, roasted young pigeon, smoked promfret, dried fried rice noodles with…

spots.name: Café One
spots.desc: Causeway Bay, Open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Fun & friendly informal dining from an open kitchen and an exciting buffet featuring a wide selection of Asian and Western cuisines.

spots.name: Tony Roma's
spots.desc: International food. This branch has the advantage of an outdoor terrace that enables you to eat and drink above the noise of the streets below.

spots.name: Under the Bridge Spicy Crab
spots.desc: This has become a Hong Kong institution that is famous for its Typhoon Shelter style crab. People come for the food not the interior which is basic.
spots.addr: Shop 1-2, G/F, 414 - 424 Jaffe Road, Causeway Bay

spots.name: West Villa Restaurant
spots.desc: Its signature dim sum is the cha xiu bao (叉燒包) or roast pork buns that is served steamed, fried or as rolls. One of the items is named "Big Brother Chaxiu" after Hong Kong's film star Jacky Chan (Big Brother) who is fond of its cha xiu buns.

spots.name: Fook Lam Moon
spots.desc: The main branch of an old school Cantonese restaurant group with locations in Kowloon, Shanghai and Japan. Famous for luxurious delicacies such as abalone, and swallow's nest. More affordable specialties include roast suckling pig, crispy chicken, and steamed lotus leaf rice.

spots.name: The Coffee Academics
spots.desc: Great coffee a short walk from Times Square in Causeway bay. Coffee is roasted on premise and they have an outside sitting area.
spots.addr: G/F, Bigfoot Centre, 38 Yiu Wa St

spots.name: The Cafe Corridor
spots.desc: Small coffee shop directly opposite Time Square. Entrance is really small so look carefully. Good coffee for $26.

spots.name: The Pawn
spots.desc: Wan Chai. A Western-style bar and cafe in an attractive building that was once a pawn shop. It is away from the naughty parts of Wan Chai in one of the few historic buildings remaining in Hong Kong. It will appeal to visitors seeking a good range of imported beers and wines.

spots.name: Joe Bananas
spots.desc: This is one Hong Kong's most famous and popular bars, and can be highly recommended to younger travellers. Drinks are competitively priced, and staff are helpful and friendly.

spots.name: Carnegie's
spots.desc: Rock music themed bar. Live bands playing occasionally, sports on multiple screens and a big screen, dancing the night away on the bar top.

spots.name: The Wanch
spots.desc: A good bar for music lovers with live music playing every night. There is also a showcase of local bands held over several days around the 1st of July every year.

spots.name: The Jockey
spots.desc: A relaxed British style pub that serves food. When the weather suits this is a great place to sit outside and watch the world pass by.

spots.name: Moon Garden Tea House
spots.desc: A calming location in a busy part of town where you can choose from over 70 types of tea and, for a price, enjoy the Chinese ritual of tea served in tiny cups. Food is also served.

spots.name: Dickens Bar
spots.desc: Popular British-style sports bar in the basement of the Excelsior hotel. A good range of drinks and serves very good English food, including a notable curry lunch buffet.

spots.name: Cheung Chau
spots.desc: A traditional community based on an active fishing fleet and many thriving seafood restaurants. It has a number of reasonable hiking trails and some usable beaches.

spots.name: Peng Chau
spots.desc: Although it has a reputation for being dull and lacking in tourist attractions, you may be nevertheless be pleasantly surprised. Restaurants here are cheaper than the other islands and you get the feeling you are off the 'beaten-track' of mass tourism. Perhaps it is the place to go at the end of your holiday when you are weary of the fast-pace of the big city and just want to slow down, have a…

spots.name: Lamma Island
spots.desc: Has become increasingly popular with Western hippies who have created their own small residential community in Yung Shue Wan (榕樹灣). On both sides of the island you will find attractive bars, restaurants and cafes, making it a popular destination for local Chinese people out on a day trip.

spots.name: Po Toi islands
spots.desc: Around 3km south of Hong Kong island. The Po Toi Islands are about six small island where only Po Toi Island is inhabited. However, during the fishing season there may be around six thousand people living around the islands. The most famous seafood on Po Toi are octopus and "Ma You" Fish (馬鮪魚). Go to Po Toi Island to see the famous rock formations and eat good seafood. You are advised to reserve…

spots.name: Soko islands
spots.desc: Found in the southwest of the Hong Kong SAR. They comprise seven small islands and nine sets of reefs. Today, these islands are uninhabited but in the distant past they were home to many people.

spots.name: Tap Mun Chau
spots.desc: Also known as Grass Island, is in the North East of the territory. It has about 100 residents, mostly fishermen. Its main attraction is its isolation and quality seafood restaurant that was made famous by the patronage of Hong Kong's last governor, Chris Patten.

spots.name: Tung Lung Chau
spots.desc: Meaning 'east dragon island' in Cantonese, it is found off Clearwater Bay. It has another name: 'Nam Tong island' (南堂島).

spots.name: Tung Ping Chau
spots.desc: Found in the North East of Hong Kong, in Mirs Bay (大鵬灣). Today, Tung Ping Chau does not have many residents, however, it used to be a very important island during the war between Japan and China. Then it was an important underground transport route between China and Hong Kong. It was also used by the British military and others who were fighting against Japan. In its heyday, there were 10…

spots.name: Kwo Chau islands
spots.desc: Located to the east of Hong Kong island. There are three main islands and 29 small islands. The Kwo Chau Islands look like a bowl of fruit from the air and so this is how they got their name. Likewise, the three main islands look like nine pins from the sky, hence the name. Individually, they are known as East Ninepin Island (Tung Kwo Chau), South Ninepin Island (Nam Kwo Chau) and North Ninepin…

spots.name: Mo Tat (Old Village)
spots.desc: Located a short walk inland from the coastal village of Mo Tat Wan, across the low ridge, Mo Tat is a rare example of an old Hong Kong village with both its original layout and traditional architecture fully intact, in contrast to many other such villages around the country where the houses have been redeveloped into more modern multi-storey units. The traditional Chinese-style houses are also…

spots.name: Walk between the main towns
spots.desc: The walk between Yung Shue Wan and Sok Kwu Wan is pleasant and not too challenging. Maybe plan 60 to 90 minutes to get across. Mo Tat Wan is another 30 minutes walk. Note in summer you should wear a hat for shade and carry plenty of water. This walk takes about an hour and is well sign posted. It passes a beach which offers swimming facilities within a shark free net and great views of the power…

spots.name: Kamikaze Caves
spots.desc: These caves near Sok Kwu Wan were apparently built by the Japanese army to hide speedboats that could attack allied ships by surprise.

spots.name: Bay
spots.desc: Restaurant and bar, which specialises in Western style seafood

spots.name: Rainbow Restaurant
spots.desc: The first, last and one in between are Rainbow restaurants with great food. A small lobster cost $140 and a small Salt and Pepper Squid cost $80. They also offer a free ferry service for customers which is a great way to see the harbour.

spots.name: The Bookworm Cafe
spots.desc: Great ambiance and tasty vegetarian food, it also provides free internet access.

spots.name: Murray House
spots.desc: One of Hong Kong's oldest colonial buildings. It was built as officer's barracks in Central then dismantled brick-by-brick in 1982. After a protracted dispute over the building's final location, it was reconstructed beside the Stanley promenade in 2001. During the building's two decades in storage markings made to the bricks to aid in the reconstruction leached off, leading to a complex…

spots.name: Tin Hau Temple
spots.desc: One of several temples in Hong Kong dedicated to Tin Hau (aka Mazu), Goddess of the Sea. The Stanley Tin Hau Temple was built in 1767.

spots.name: Dragon Boat Racing
spots.desc: Takes place in Stanley in May every year during the Tuen Ng festival (端午節).

spots.name: Repulse Bay Beach
spots.desc: Biggest and most popular beach and is suitable for families with small children.

spots.name: Middle Bay beach
spots.desc: Popular with gay men and is a 20-minute walk along the coast from Repulse Bay.

spots.name: South Bay beach
spots.desc: Never too busy, even on weekends, but you will need to take a taxi from Repulse Bay.

spots.name: Stanley Main Beach
spots.desc: A popular beach for wind-surfing, and hosts annual dragon boat races. Facilities include a café, changing rooms and showers, shark nets, public toilets and a barbeque area.

spots.name: St Stephens Beach
spots.desc: Much quieter and more secluded beach that Stanley Main Beach, but still includes a beach café, changing rooms, public toilets and showers. A barbeque area is available up the hill from the beach, and is accessible via stairs.

spots.name: Shek O Beach
spots.desc: Attracts a young Chinese crowd, especially older teenagers and young adults.

spots.name: Horizon Plaza
spots.desc: A former industrial building converted to a large 20-story factory outlet, selling fashion, home decor and antiques. Brands include Costume National, Jean-Paul Gaultier, Kookai, Jimm Choo, Armani, Vivienne Westwood and others.
spots.addr: 2 Lee Wing St, Ap Lei Chau

spots.name: Stanley Market
spots.desc: Head to Stanley Market and prepare to haggle. This is the one-stop place to buy your holiday gifts and souvenirs, albeit at higher tourist adjusted prices. There is a wide selection of ornaments, pictures, artwork and clothes to browse around. You will find a selection of both Chinese-style goods (such as ink and brushes for Chinese calligraphy) and also many western brand clothes.

spots.name: Stanley Plaza
spots.desc: The multi-story Stanley Plaza shopping centre, which links the Stanley bus stop to the main promenade.

spots.name: Chinese and Thailand Seafood Restaurant
spots.desc: Food here is reasonable and it offers probably the best meal in the village.

spots.name: Spices Restaurant
spots.desc: Serves pan-Asian food with style. Excellent location, only a few minutes walk from the beach. You can choose to dine outside on the patio and enjoy superb views over Repulse Bay.
spots.addr: G/F The Arcade, 109 Repulse Bay Road, Repulse Bay

spots.name: The Verandah
spots.desc: Posh colonial-style Western dinning recreated in a modern building overlooking Repulse Bay.

spots.name: The Boathouse
spots.desc: A reasonably inexpensive restaurant on the Stanley promenade that features dining upstairs and a more relaxed bar on the ground floor.

spots.name: The Smugglers Inn
spots.desc: Located on the sea front, this is a British-style pub that serves a range of beers and traditional English pub food. It is along the Stanley promenade, and offers a great view of the ocean while relaxing with a drink.

spots.name: Fireboat Alexander Grantham Exhibition Gallery
spots.desc: Exhibits firefighting stuff.

spots.name: Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts
spots.desc: A venue for dance, music and drama.
spots.addr: The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts 1 Gloucester Road Wanchai

spots.name: Hysan Place
spots.desc: High-end shopping mall with a food court on upper floor.

spots.name: Cityplaza
spots.desc: A large shopping centre, with an ice-skating rink.
spots.addr: 18 Taikoo Shing Road, Sai Wan Ho

spots.name: Cafe Kenon
spots.desc: Where affordable Italian food meets Chinese expectations.
spots.addr: Shop 208, 2/F Tai Yau Plaza, 181 Johnston Rd, Wanchai

spots.name: New Bangkok Restaurant
spots.desc: Friendly staff serving excellent Thai food.

spots.name: Baby Blue Cafe and Bar
spots.desc: Western food served to meet Hong Kong taste buds.
spots.addr: 3/F, Chuang's Enterprises Building, 382 Lockhart Road, Causeway Bay

spots.name: Chun Kee Restaurant
spots.desc: Serves typical Chinese food from dumplings to Peking Duck.
spots.addr: 117-119 Shau Kei Wan Road, Sai Wan Ho

spots.name: Devils Advocate
spots.desc: Popular with the rugby crowd with English pub food.

spots.name: Kangaroo Pub
spots.desc: Australian sports bar. Has a book exchange.

spots.name: The Canny Man
spots.desc: Scottish style Whiskey Bar with a free pool table.

spots.name: Skitz Sports Bar
spots.desc: 5/F. Sports bar with pool tables, darts and big screens.

spots.name: The Chapel
spots.desc: Serves curry.

spots.name: Inn Side Out
spots.desc: Also 'East End Brewing Company'.

spots.name: Waglan island
spots.desc: Near Po Toi, is famous for its lighthouse.

spots.name: Peach Garden
spots.desc: Small family owned seafood restaurant

spots.name: Big Wave Bay
spots.desc: Popular surf and swimming beach with restaurants and bars.

spots.name: Space Warehouse
spots.desc: Brands such as Prada and Helmut Lang.
spots.addr: 2/F Marina Square, East Commercial Block, Ap Lei Chau

spots.name: Man Mo Temple Compound
spots.desc: Consists of Man Mo Temple, Lit Shing Kung Temple and Kung Sor assembly hall. Man Mo Temple was built in the 1840s and is Hong Kong Island's oldest temple. It is nestled amongst antique shops, with the air full of smoke from hundreds of burning incense coils. While you are there, pop into one of the many antique shops to see some of the best Chinese and South-East Asian antiques in the world, and…

spots.name: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
spots.desc: Museum of teapots and cups, with exhibits ranging from modern to 3000 years old.

spots.name: Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences
spots.desc: The neighbour of one of the earliest hospitals in Hong Kong, Tung Wah Hospital, this museum shows how the healthcare system evolved from traditional Chinese medicine to modern Western medicine, via the establishment of numerous hospitals and the first medical school (now the University of Hong Kong), of which Dr. Sun Yat-sen was a student.

spots.name: Hong Kong Visual Arts Centre
spots.desc: Offers visual arts studios for artists as well as exhibition halls.

spots.name: Madame Tussaud's
spots.desc: The usual Tussaud's waxworks with characters that appeal to Chinese interests.

spots.name: University Museum and Art Gallery
spots.desc: The oldest museum in Hong Kong dating back to 1953 has a large permanent collection of Chinese antiquities as well as modern paintings. It also host exhibitions of contemporary and ancient art.

spots.name: Hong Kong Maritime Museum
spots.desc: In addition to original artifacts, cannons, scrolls, ship's models and paintings, the galleries of Hong Kong Maritime Museum have over 25 interactive screens using the latest technology to introduce visitors to the vast range of stories and topics at the heart of Hong Kong's – and the world's – maritime story. You can learn of Poon Lim, the world record holder for solo survival at sea. See how a…
spots.price: $30, half price for seniors and students

spots.name: Trick Eye Museum Hong Kong
spots.desc: The only Korean 3D museum in Hong Kong. It presents a magnificent collection of 3D art pieces. It features paintings on plain surfaces that magically appear to be three dimensional through the use of optical illusion. You are most welcome to touch, climb and interact with the amazing exhibits. You can also enjoy the free observation deck view of the beautiful Harbour View.
spots.addr: Level 3, The Peak Galleria, 118 Peak Road, The Peak

spots.name: Chater Garden
spots.desc: Adjacent to the Legislative Council Building, this is the place where disgruntled Hongkongers come to protest. Named after businessman Sir Paul Chater.

spots.name: Lung Fu Shan Country Park
spots.desc: Hong Kong newest and smallest Country Park. Its proximity to the Peak makes it highly accessible and one is rewarded by a pleasant hike away from the crowds nearby. A convenient place to make a BBQ with great views over Victoria Harbour. Budding military historians will enjoy exploring Pinewood battery and other remnants of the Second World War.

spots.name: Mount Davis
spots.desc: Walk up Mount Davis to see the abandoned Second World War-era gunnery fortifications. Take the steps up from Victoria Rd just west of Kennedy Town; or follow Victoria Rd until you reach the roundabout (about a kilometre), and take the mountain road up. The climb will take a while, but there are many ruins to explore, and great views. There's also a youth hostel at the top if you are too tired to…

spots.name: Wellington St
spots.desc: Nice street with dried foodstuffs, various restaurants, majong pieces. Also check out Art Jam at 123 Wellington St. They provide you with canvas, paints and materials. From $200 to $500 depending on when you go and canvas size.

spots.name: Flow
spots.desc: Second-hand bookshop where you can exchange your used travel guides.

spots.name: IFC Mall
spots.desc: Sleek and impressive, this is one of the most prestigious shopping centres on the island. Here you will find one of the best cinemas with the added bonus that the film will be the English language version (if it is an animation). Go up to the rooftop and you will find yourself in public open space. The views of Victoria Harbour are good and you will find a couple of bars that will help you enjoy…

spots.name: The Landmark
spots.desc: An older shopping centre that has had a facelift to incorporate a five-star hotel. For many, it remains a focus for many of the most expensive designer fashion shops in Hong Kong.

spots.name: Pedder St and Queen's Rd
spots.desc: One of the best locations for jewellery and designer watches at prices that can be up to 35% less than Europe. As always, shop around for the best prices and always buy from reputable dealers to avoid fake goods.

spots.name: Pacific Place and Queensway and Admiralty Centre
spots.desc: A number of interconnected shopping malls connected to Admiralty MTR. Pleasant air-conditioned shopping for mid-price to expensive branded goods and restaurants.

spots.name: Soho and south of Hollywood Rd area
spots.desc: Has a trendy shopping area around Staunton and Lower Elgin St with lots of local designers.

spots.name: The Lanes
spots.desc: Buy silks, fabrics, Chinese dresses, watches, leather bags and many other things here. Despite its prime location close to Central MTR, these narrow streets have a reputation among locals for quality goods at competitive prices.

spots.name: Cat Street
spots.desc: Probably the best place to buy souvenirs, lots of Mao memorabilia, porcelain, Buddha statues and "antiques". Lok Ku Rd, walk down Hollywood Rd towards the west, when you see the Man Mo temple walk down the stairs on the right hand side.

spots.name: Man Wa Lane
